transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, hi. Thank you for seeing me. I... gosh, where to start. I guess what finally brought me in is that I just really don't feel like myself anymore. Not at all. It’s hard to explain, but I’ve always been such a busy, engaged person. I mean, working as a teaching assistant takes a lot of energy, the kids keep you on your toes, but I always, always made time for the things I loved. 

I used to do a lot of painting—mostly watercolors, just sitting by the window for hours trying to get the light right. And I loved hiking. There’s a trail near my house I used to do every single weekend without fail. Plus I was in a local choir, and I was always the one organizing our big Sunday family gatherings. I was just always doing something, always looking forward to the next thing. 

But lately... I don't know. Now, even when I have a completely free hour, or a whole Saturday afternoon where I could be doing any of those things, I just sit there. I look at my paintbrushes or my hiking boots by the door and I am just completely unable to care about any of it. I just sit in a chair in the living room and stare, really. I can't even muster up the interest to care about missing choir practice or skipping the Sunday dinners, which used to be the highlight of my week. It’s like the color has just drained out of everything I used to love, and I just don't know where the old me went. I used to be so passionate about my hobbies, you know? And now it's just... nothing. I just sit there.
Do you feel sad most of the time?

Sad is... I mean, yes, I suppose sad is the word, but it feels so much bigger and heavier than just regular sadness. It’s almost like... well, most days I feel like there's this thick, heavy gray film over absolutely everything in my life. It just coats everything. And it really doesn't even matter where I am or what's going on around me, the feeling just won't budge. 

I could be standing right in the middle of a classroom full of students—and you know how loud and chaotic a room full of kids can get, there's always someone needing help with an assignment or talking out of turn or dropping a textbook—but I can be right there in the thick of all that noise and activity, and I just feel completely hollow inside. Just totally empty. Or even at home, I can be sitting right next to my husband on our own couch, just trying to have a normal, quiet evening together like we've done a million times, and I still feel that exact same hollowness. And I'm just... I'm constantly hovering right on the edge of crying. I'll just be standing there in the school hallway or sitting in my own kitchen, feeling so incredibly close to tears, and I have to swallow hard to fight them back. It's just this constant, heavy weight that never really lifts, no matter how hard I try to push through it and act normal for the students or for my husband.
Do you still enjoy things you used to like, even if you can't muster the energy to do them?

Well, like I was trying to explain earlier with the painting and the hiking... it really isn't just an energy thing. I mean, yes, being a teaching assistant drains you, but even if you sat me down and did all the prep work for me, the actual feeling of liking those things is just... gone. 

For example, my husband actually tried this just the other weekend. He knows how much I used to love my watercolors, so he brought my whole kit into the living room. He set up the paper, got the little cups of water, laid out all my favorite brushes—everything. All I had to do was lift my hand and paint. And I just stared at it. I didn't feel even a tiny spark of that joy I used to get. I used to get so excited just seeing the colors bleed into the paper, trying to capture the way the light comes through our living room window, you know? It used to make me feel so peaceful and happy. But looking at it the other day, I just felt completely blank. I didn't care at all. 

So it really isn't just that I'm too tired to put my hiking boots on or drive to choir practice. It's that when I think about the choir, or those big Sunday family dinners I used to spend days planning and looking forward to, I don't even *want* to do them anymore. The enjoyment itself is just completely missing. I can have a totally free hour, with absolutely no grading or chores to do, just sitting there looking at the things that used to define who I was, and I can't even force myself to care about them. It's like the part of me that knows how to enjoy things just turned off.
How long have you been feeling this way?

Well, gosh... let me think. It hasn't always been like this, obviously, but it definitely feels like it's been a really long time now. I'd say... well, it's been building for about eight months now. Yes, right around eight months. I can actually pinpoint it pretty well because it started right around the time I took over the STEM-Arts curriculum initiative at the school. 

You see, they wanted to integrate more creative projects into the science and math classes, and since everyone knew I was the "artsy" teaching assistant who painted and sang in the choir, they asked me to spearhead the whole thing. I was so flattered at first! I spent weeks drawing up these elaborate lesson plans, trying to figure out how to use watercolor techniques to teach the kids about capillary action in plants, things like that. I was staying late, pouring over these ideas, talking to the science teachers... and it was a lot of pressure, making sure it aligned with the state standards while still being engaging for the kids. 

And somewhere in the middle of all that planning and coordinating and trying to get everyone on board, I just started feeling... well, like I was wading through mud. I thought I was just stressed about the initiative, you know? Just typical work stress. I kept telling myself, "Once the first quarter is over and the teachers are comfortable with the new lesson plans, I'll bounce back. I'll get back to my own painting, I'll get back to the Sunday dinners." But the initiative launched, and it actually went really well, the kids loved it... but I never bounced back. The heavy feeling just stayed, and then it got worse, and now here we are, eight months later, and I'm just sitting in my living room staring at the wall. So, yes, about eight months since it all really started creeping in.
Are there any activities that you still find pleasure in?

Well, that's... that's the thing. That's actually what finally made me realize I needed to come see someone. Because the short answer is no. There really isn't anything anymore. 

I mean, I've been trying so hard to find just one thing, just one little spark of something that feels good, but it's like I don't even feel like myself anymore. Like I was saying before about the watercolors and the hiking... those weren't just hobbies, you know? They were who I was. I was the woman who painted the landscapes, the one who organized the big Sunday family gatherings. Oh, those gatherings used to be such a production! I would spend all week planning the menu, going to the specialty grocery store across town just to get the right kind of cheese or the perfect cut of meat. I'd be on my feet for hours on Sunday morning, chopping and stirring and setting the table with my good plates. And I loved every single second of it. I loved the noise when everyone arrived, I loved the smell of the house, I loved the feeling of feeding the people I care about. 

And the choir, too! I used to look forward to Wednesday night rehearsals all week long. Just the feeling of all those voices blending together, standing in the alto section and hitting that perfect harmony... it would just lift me right up, no matter how hard my week at school had been. 

But now? Now, I can have a completely free hour on a Sunday afternoon, or a Wednesday evening where I don't have a single paper to grade or a single chore to do, and I just... sit there. I just sit in my chair in the living room. I don't even turn on the television most of the time. I just sit there and I can't bring myself to care about any of it. Not the painting, not the hiking trails, not the choir, not the family dinners. It's all just... gone. And it's terrifying, honestly, to look at all the pieces of your life that used to make you who you are, and just feel absolutely nothing towards them. So, no, doctor, there really isn't anything I find pleasure in right now. I just sit there unable to care.
Are there any small, everyday things that still bring you a little bit of pleasure?

Well, that's... I mean, I know you're trying to find a silver lining, like maybe a cup of coffee or a hot shower or something, but... no. It really is just... nothing. 

And I know I'm repeating myself, I'm sorry, I just... I really need you to understand how absolute this is. It's not just that I don't want to do the big things anymore. It's the small things, too. Like, I used to love the drive to school in the mornings. I'd roll the windows down a crack if it was crisp out, listen to the classical station, maybe pick up a latte from that little independent shop on the corner of Elm and 4th. The barista, Sarah, she always knew my order—a half-caf oat milk latte with just a sprinkle of cinnamon. Just that little interaction, the smell of the espresso, the warmth of the cup in my hands... that used to be a highlight of my morning. It set the tone for the whole day before I even stepped foot in the classroom. 

But now? Now I just drive in silence. I don't even bother stopping for the coffee because I know it's just going to taste like hot, wet cardboard to me anyway. I don't care about the crisp air, I don't care about the music. 

And that's... like I said, that's what finally brought me in here to see you. Because I don't feel like myself anymore. I'm just this shell of a person who used to exist. I used to be the woman who made time for painting and hiking and the choir and those huge Sunday family gatherings. I was always doing something, always finding joy in something, whether it was a big project or just a quiet morning cup of coffee. And now, even when I have a completely free hour, even when the house is quiet and there's absolutely no pressure on me to do anything at all... I just sit there. I literally just sit in the chair and I am completely unable to care about any of it. Not the big things, not the small things. Just... nothing.
Do you feel like you've lost interest in activities that you used to enjoy?

Yes... yes, exactly. I know I keep circling back to this, and I'm sorry if I'm repeating myself, but that is exactly it. That complete loss of interest is what finally brought me in here to see you. I just... I really don't feel like myself anymore, at all. 

The woman I used to be, the one who always made time for her watercolor painting, the one who was out hiking on the trails every weekend, who sang her heart out in the choir and orchestrated those massive Sunday family gatherings... she just feels completely gone. It's not just that I'm too tired to do those things, though I am tired, it's that the actual desire to do them has been completely wiped out. 

Like I was saying before, I can have a perfectly free hour now. An hour where the house is quiet, the school day is over, the grading is done, and I could do absolutely anything I want... and I just sit there. I sit in my chair in the living room, and I am completely unable to care about any of it. I'll look over at my paintbrushes sitting on the desk, or I'll see my hiking boots by the front door, and there's just... nothing. No spark, no interest, no pull to go pick them up. Just this heavy, empty feeling where all my passion used to be.
Have you noticed any significant changes in your weight recently?

Weight? Um... no, not really. I mean, I haven't noticed anything significant, anyway. I know sometimes people eat a lot when they're upset, or they stop eating entirely, but... my clothes still fit the same as they did before this whole... whatever this is... started. 

I guess I'm still eating, mostly because I know I have to, right? Like, my husband will make dinner and I'll sit at the table and chew and swallow, but it's not like I'm enjoying it. Like I was saying about the Sunday dinners I used to make... I used to care so much about the flavors, the presentation, all of it. Now, it's just fuel. It could be a gourmet meal or a piece of dry toast, and it's all the same to me. But no, to answer your question, my weight hasn't really gone up or down. I step on the scale in the bathroom sometimes—it's this old digital one we've had for years, the kind where you have to tap it with your foot to wake it up first—and the number is pretty much exactly what it's been for the last five years. So, no changes there, even though everything else in my life feels completely turned upside down.
Have you been having trouble sleeping?

Sleep? Oh, my sleep has been just... it's been a complete disaster. It's been all over the place for months now, long before I even realized how bad everything else was getting. 

I mean, I'll go to bed, right? I'll do my whole routine—wash my face, brush my teeth, put on my pajamas, get into bed around ten-thirty or eleven, just like I always have. But then I just lie there. I lie there in the dark, staring at the ceiling, and my brain just will not shut off. It's like it's on this endless loop, replaying everything. And the weird thing is, it's not even always about school, though sometimes it is. Sometimes I'm lying there replaying all these details for this grant application the lead teacher and I were working on—which is ridiculous, because I don't even care about the grant anymore, like I told you, I don't care about any of it. But my brain just spins and spins on it anyway. 

And then, if I do finally manage to drift off, it's never for the whole night. I almost always wake up around three or four in the morning. I'll look at the clock—it's this digital clock with red numbers on my nightstand—and it'll say 3:14 or 4:02, and I just know, I know in my bones that I'm not going back to sleep. I'll toss and turn, try adjusting the pillows, try kicking off the blankets, but I'm just wide awake. And the worst part is, even on the rare nights where I do manage to sleep a little longer, maybe I get six or seven hours... I wake up feeling like I never even closed my eyes. I get up and I feel just as exhausted, just as heavy and drained as I did when I went to bed. It's like the sleep doesn't even do anything anymore. It's just... it's exhausting, honestly. It's like I can't find rest anywhere, not during the day when I'm just sitting in my chair, and definitely not at night.
Have you been having any thoughts about hurting yourself?

Hurting myself? Um... I... I don't know if I'd use those exact words, but... well, yes. Yes, I suppose I have. It's... it's really hard to talk about. I haven't even wanted to admit it to myself, honestly. 

But, like I was saying about how I just sit there in my chair during the day, or how I lie awake at night staring at the ceiling? Sometimes, especially on those really bad nights, or... or actually, sometimes I'll go into my art studio. I know I said I don't paint anymore, and I don't, but sometimes I just go in there and sit. It used to be my favorite room in the house. It has this big window that looks out over the backyard, and I used to love the light in there. But now I just sit there late at night, and... and I catch myself thinking that it would just be so much easier if it all stopped. 

I think... I think about how it would just be such a profound relief if I went to sleep and just... didn't wake up. Just didn't have to face another day of feeling this heavy, this empty. It's not that I want to violently hurt myself, I haven't... I haven't sat down and written out a note or figured out a way to do it, I don't have a specific plan or anything like that. But the thoughts are there. They just creep in, especially when it's quiet and everyone else is asleep. And they're so persistent. 

It really scares me, to be perfectly honest with you. It terrifies me that my brain is even going to those places. I've always been the strong one, the one holding everything together for the family, the one organizing the Sunday dinners and keeping the school schedule running smoothly. And to have these thoughts... it got to the point where I finally broke down and told my husband. We were sitting in the kitchen last week, he was making coffee, and I just started crying and told him I couldn't keep handling these thoughts all by myself anymore. That's a big part of why he pushed me to finally make this appointment. So... yes, I guess the short answer is yes, I've been having those kinds of thoughts, and they really, really frighten me.
Do you feel like you're moving more slowly than you used to?

Moving more slowly? Um... I don't know. I don't think so? I mean, I feel heavy, like I mentioned before, like everything takes so much effort. When I get up from that chair in the living room, it feels like I'm dragging a hundred pounds of sand with me. But as for actually moving in slow motion or anything like that... no, I haven't really noticed that. 

I guess I'm just doing less overall, so there's less moving to do. Like, at school, I used to be the one darting around the classroom, handing out papers, helping the kids with their coats, practically running down the hall to the supply closet and back before the bell rang. I was always on my feet, always moving. Now, when I'm there, I just kind of sit at the little desk in the back. I'll get up if the lead teacher specifically asks me to hand something out, but I'm not buzzing around the way I used to. But when I do walk, I think I'm walking at a normal pace? My husband hasn't said anything about me moving like a snail or anything. 

It's more just... the motivation to move is gone. Like the other day, I dropped a pen in the kitchen. It just rolled under the edge of the fridge. Before, I would have just bent down, grabbed it, and put it back in the drawer without a second thought. But I just stood there looking at it for what felt like five minutes, trying to convince myself it was worth the effort to bend over and pick it up. I eventually did, but it just felt like such a monumental task. But the actual physical movement of bending down? I think that was normal. So, no, I wouldn't say I'm physically moving slower, just... doing a lot less of it.
Do you feel like your body is moving more slowly than usual?

Um, I think that's kind of what I was just trying to explain a second ago... about not really moving in slow motion. My actual body parts, like my arms and legs, they still work at the normal speed when I finally get them going. It's just getting them to start that's the problem. 

Like, just yesterday morning, I was in the kitchen while my husband was making breakfast. He had put some bread in the toaster, and I was just standing there waiting for the butter to soften. And when the toast popped up, I reached over to grab it, and my hand moved just as fast as it always has, you know? I didn't reach for it like I was underwater or anything weird like that. But the whole time, I was just thinking about how exhausted I was just standing there by the counter. The kitchen tiles felt so hard under my feet, and I was just staring at the toaster crumbs on the counter, thinking about how I should wipe them up, but I just couldn't bring myself to walk the three steps to the sink to get the sponge. 

But if you're asking if my actual physical movements are delayed or sluggish once I'm actually in motion... no, I really don't think they are. I haven't noticed anyone looking at me strangely or asking why I'm walking so slow. It's really just that internal feeling of everything being so much work, like I said before. Not the actual speed of my body.
Do you feel guilty about anything in particular?

Guilty? Oh, God, yes. Constantly. It's... it's like this heavy blanket that just sits on my chest all day. It's actually one of the worst parts of all of this, to be honest. 

I don't know if I mentioned this, but I'm a teaching assistant, and lately, I've been helping the lead teacher with this new curriculum project for the kids. It's supposed to be this really engaging, hands-on science unit. And... well, whenever anything goes wrong with it, even the tiniest little thing, I just spiral. Like last Tuesday, we were missing a few of the specialized magnets we needed for a demonstration. It wasn't even my job to order them, the office was supposed to handle the supplies, but I just stood there in the classroom, looking at the kids' faces, and I felt this overwhelming, crushing sense of guilt. 

I just keep thinking that I'm completely letting the students down. They deserve someone who is sharp and on top of things, someone who can make sure their day goes perfectly, and instead, they have me, just barely holding it together in the back of the room. And it goes deeper than that, too. It's not just the students. It's... it's my parents. 

They worked so incredibly hard to put me through college. My dad picked up extra shifts, my mom was always saving every penny, just so I could get my Bachelor's degree and have a good career in education. They made all these sacrifices so I could have this opportunity, and now look at me. I'm 49 years old, I'm just an assistant, and I can't even manage to get through a simple science project without feeling like a total failure. I feel like I'm just wasting everything they did for me. It's this constant loop in my head—I'm a disappointment to the kids, I'm a disappointment to my parents, I'm just... not good enough. And even when my husband tells me I'm being ridiculous, that it's just a few missing magnets, I can't shake it. The guilt just eats away at me, all the time.
Do you feel like you're resting or sleeping more than usual?

Resting more? I... gosh, I wish I was. I mean, I might be physically in the bed more, but I'm definitely not resting. My sleep has actually been completely all over the place for months now. It's like the second my head hits the pillow, my brain just decides it's time to go into overdrive. 

I'll just lie there in the dark, staring at the shadows on the ceiling, and I can't stop my mind from racing. I end up just lying awake replaying all the grant details for that new science curriculum I was telling you about, worrying about the funding for the supplies and whether I filled out the requisition forms exactly right, going over the numbers in my head over and over again. And it takes forever to finally drift off. 

But then, even when I do finally fall asleep, it doesn't last. I almost always wake up around three or four in the morning. It's like clockwork. The house is pitch black, my husband is sound asleep next to me, and my eyes just snap open. I'll look at the red numbers on the alarm clock and just feel this dread, knowing I'm going to be awake for the rest of the night. And the most frustrating part of it all is that on the weekends, I'll try to make up for it. I'll tell myself, 'Okay, just stay in bed, just try to get a few more hours.' But even when I do manage to sleep longer on a Saturday, I get up feeling like I never rested at all. It's like I spent the whole night running a marathon. I finally drag myself out from under the covers to go make coffee, and I'm just as bone-tired as I was when I went to sleep. So, no, I'm definitely not getting more rest. I'm just spending more time being exhausted.
Do you feel like your life is worth living?

Worth living? I... um. That's a really hard question. It's... well, it's complicated. I don't know if I'd say I actively want to die, like, I don't want to hurt myself or anything. But... there are these moments. 

Like I was saying about how I'm just lying awake at night, staring at the ceiling and worrying about the science curriculum and the grants and the kids and my parents... sometimes, when it's just so quiet and the house is completely still, and I'm just so, so tired of the racing thoughts and the guilt and the exhaustion... I catch myself thinking that it would just be so much easier if I didn't wake up. If I could just drift off and not have to face the next day, not have to drag myself out of bed and pretend I'm okay in front of a classroom full of children. It just feels like it would be such a relief, you know? Just to have the quiet. To have it all stop. 

I haven't actually made a plan or anything. I don't have, like, a specific idea of how I would do it, and I wouldn't want to put my husband through that. He's been so patient with me, even when I'm being completely unreasonable about things like the toaster crumbs or the missing magnets. But those thoughts... they just creep in. Especially when I'm working late, trying to catch up on things for the lead teacher, and I'm just sitting there in the dark. It really scares me, to be honest. It scares me that my brain even goes there. That's actually... that's a big part of why I'm here. I finally broke down and told my husband about it a few weeks ago. I just told him, 'I can't keep handling these thoughts alone anymore.' It was terrifying to say out loud, but I just felt like I was drowning in it, and I needed him to know how bad it had gotten. So... yeah. It's not that I don't want to live, exactly. It's just that sometimes, living feels like too much work.
Have you experienced any significant changes in your appetite?

Appetite? Oh, um... well, no, not really. I mean, nothing significant, I don't think. It's funny you ask, though, because my husband was just asking me the other day if I liked the new brand of pasta he bought, and I had to tell him I honestly hadn't even noticed a difference. Which is unusual for me, because I usually love a good penne, you know? But lately, food is just... it's just food. 

I still eat my regular meals, mostly. I'll have a piece of toast or a bowl of oatmeal before I head out to the school in the morning, and I usually pack a sandwich or a salad for lunch. Sometimes I don't quite finish it, especially if the kids are having a particularly chaotic day and I have to spend my lunch break helping the lead teacher reorganize the classroom or clean up whatever mess happened during the morning activities. And dinner... well, dinner is just whatever my husband puts in front of me. He's been doing most of the cooking lately, bless him, because by the time I get home, I'm just so drained. 

But I haven't noticed any major changes in how much I'm eating, and my clothes still fit exactly the same. I weigh myself every Sunday morning—it's just a habit I've had for years—and the number on the scale hasn't really moved more than a pound or two in either direction. So, no, I wouldn't say my appetite has changed significantly. It's just that the joy of eating, the actual enjoyment of the flavors and looking forward to a meal... that's kind of just disappeared, along with everything else. But I'm still eating, so... yeah, no big changes there.
Have you experienced any periods of feeling somewhat better over the past eight months?

Feeling better? I... um. No. No, not really. It's actually kind of eerie that you specifically say eight months, because... well, that's exactly it. It hasn't been like a wave where it comes and goes, or where I have a good week and then a bad week. It's just been this constant, steady weight that’s been building for about eight months now. 

That was right around the time... well, the school decided to launch this new STEM-Arts curriculum initiative. The lead teacher I work with was already completely overwhelmed with the standardized testing prep, so the principal pulled me aside and asked if I could take over the initiative. Which, you know, I have my bachelor's degree, I'm certainly capable of doing the administrative work, and I originally thought it would be this wonderful creative outlet for the kids, a way to mix science and art together. But the logistics of it... coordinating all the different modules, ordering the specific supplies, figuring out how to stretch the grant money like I was mentioning before... it was just a massive undertaking for a teaching assistant. 

And honestly, ever since I took over that STEM-Arts initiative eight months ago, this feeling has just been building and building. I kept telling myself, 'Oh, it'll get easier once the first quarter's lesson plans are finalized,' or 'I'll feel better after we get through the parent-teacher conferences,' but I never did. I never got that relief. The stress and this... this heavy, exhausting feeling just kept piling up, day after day. Even on the days where maybe the kids do a really great job building their little engineering projects, and I should be happy or proud of them, I just stand in the back of the classroom feeling completely hollowed out. I just look at the clock and calculate how many hours until I can go back to bed. So, no, I haven't had any periods where I felt better. It’s really just been a straight line down since I took on that curriculum.
Can you describe the intensity of your feelings of sadness or emptiness, is it mild, moderate, or severe most of the time?

Moderate, I'd say. Or... well, maybe it's hard to put a label on it, but moderate sounds about right. It's not like I'm screaming or crying hysterically all day, but it's just... it's always there. 

Most days, I feel like there's this heavy, gray film over everything. It's like looking at the world through a dirty window, you know? Like, the sun might be shining outside, and the kids might be running around on the playground, laughing and playing, and I can see that they're happy, but I can't feel any of it. I can just be standing right there in the middle of a classroom full of students, or even just sitting at the kitchen table at home with my husband while he's telling me about his day at work, and I still just feel completely hollow inside. 

It's this deep, aching emptiness that just sits right in the middle of my chest. And it's so close to the surface, too. Like, I'll be helping a student mix paint for an art project, or I'll be sorting through the recycling bin to find materials for the STEM modules, and suddenly I just feel so incredibly close to tears. For absolutely no reason! Nothing bad even happened, but the tears are just right there, prickling behind my eyes, and it takes so much energy just to blink them back and keep a straight face for the kids. It’s exhausting, really, carrying that around all the time. It just drains the color out of everything. So, yes, moderate, I suppose, because I can still function, but it's a very heavy, constant sort of sadness.
Would you say the feelings of sadness or emptiness you've been experiencing are mild, moderate, or severe most of the time?

Oh, um... well, like I was just saying a moment ago, I really do think "moderate" is probably the best word for it, if I have to pick one of those three. I'm sorry if I didn't explain it clearly enough just now, I know I tend to ramble a bit when I get going. My husband always teases me that I take the long way around a story. 

But yes, moderate. Because, as I was trying to explain, it's not this severe, bed-ridden kind of thing where I can't physically move, but most days I really do feel like there's this heavy, gray film over everything. It's just exactly like I was describing—I can be standing right there in a classroom full of students, surrounded by twenty-five kids, or I can be sitting at home with my husband, and I still just feel completely hollow. 

It never really leaves me, that feeling of being so, so close to tears. They're just constantly right there in the back of my throat, no matter where I am or who I'm talking to. So, I guess that's why I'd call it moderate. It's always there, coloring everything gray and making me feel so empty, even if I'm technically still showing up to work and doing what I'm supposed to do. Does that make sense? I just don't want to give you the wrong impression and make it sound mild, because it certainly doesn't feel mild to me, it feels incredibly heavy to carry around all day... but I'm also not completely incapacitated by it, so moderate just seems to fit best.
Would you describe your current feelings of sadness or emptiness as severe?

I... I feel like maybe we're going in circles a little bit? Or maybe I'm just not explaining myself very well, which happens, I know I tend to use a lot of words when a few would do. But no, I wouldn't say severe. Like I was just trying to explain, I'd really stick with moderate. Severe makes it sound like I'm completely bedridden and can't function at all, which isn't the case. 

But it is exactly what I was just describing to you—most days I really do feel like there's this heavy, gray film draped over absolutely everything in my life. It doesn't matter where I am or what I'm doing. I can be standing right in the middle of a classroom full of students, surrounded by all that noise and energy and chaos, or I can be sitting quietly at home on the couch with my husband, and I still just feel entirely hollow inside. And that feeling of being so, so close to tears... it's just always there, right behind my eyes, just waiting to spill over even when nothing has actually gone wrong. Worth living? I... um. That's a really hard question. It's... well, it's complicated. I don't know if I'd say I actively want to die, like, I don't want to hurt myself or anything. But... there are these moments. 

Like I was saying about how I'm just lying awake at night, staring at the ceiling and worrying about the science curriculum and the grants and the kids and my parents... sometimes, when it's just so quiet and the house is completely still, and I'm just so, so tired of the racing thoughts and the guilt and the exhaustion... I catch myself thinking that it would just be so much easier if I didn't wake up. If I could just drift off and not have to face the next day, not have to drag myself out of bed and pretend I'm okay in front of a classroom full of children. It just feels like it would be such a relief, you know? Just to have the quiet. To have it all stop. 

I haven't actually made a plan or anything. I don't have, like, a specific idea of how I would do it, and I wouldn't want to put my husband through that. He's been so patient with me, even when I'm being completely unreasonable about things like the toaster crumbs or the missing magnets. But those thoughts... they just creep in. Especially when I'm working late, trying to catch up on things for the lead teacher, and I'm just sitting there in the dark. It really scares me, to be honest. It scares me that my brain even goes there. That's actually... that's a big part of why I'm here. I finally broke down and told my husband about it a few weeks ago. I just told him, 'I can't keep handling these thoughts alone anymore.' It was terrifying to say out loud, but I just felt like I was drowning in it, and I needed him to know how bad it had gotten. So... yeah. It's not that I don't want to live, exactly. It's just that sometimes, living feels like too much work.

Appetite? Oh, um... well, no, not really. I mean, nothing significant, I don't think. Which is unusual for me, because I usually love a good penne, you know? But lately, food is just... it's just food. 

I still eat my regular meals, mostly. I'll have a piece of toast or a bowl of oatmeal before I head out to the school in the morning, and I usually pack a sandwich or a salad for lunch. Sometimes I don't quite finish it, especially if the kids are having a particularly chaotic day and I have to spend my lunch break helping the lead teacher reorganize the classroom or clean up whatever mess happened during the morning activities. And dinner... well, dinner is just whatever my husband puts in front of me. He's been doing most of the cooking lately, bless him, because by the time I get home, I'm just so drained.

I weigh myself every Sunday morning—it's just a habit I've had for years—and the number on the scale hasn't really moved more than a pound or two in either direction. So, no, I wouldn't say my appetite has changed significantly. It's just that the joy of eating, the actual enjoyment of the flavors and looking forward to a meal... that's kind of just disappeared, along with everything else. patient.answer:
Feeling better? I... um. No. No, not really. It's actually kind of eerie that you specifically say eight months, because... well, that's exactly it. It hasn't been like a wave where it comes and goes, or where I have a good week and then a bad week. It's just been this constant, steady weight that’s been building for about eight months now. 

That was right around the time... well, the school decided to launch this new STEM-Arts curriculum initiative. The lead teacher I work with was already completely overwhelmed with the standardized testing prep, so the principal pulled me aside and asked if I could take over the initiative. Which, you know, I have my bachelor's degree, I'm certainly capable of doing the administrative work, and I originally thought it would be this wonderful creative outlet for the kids, a way to mix science and art together. But the logistics of it... coordinating all the different modules, ordering the specific supplies, figuring out how to stretch the grant money like I was mentioning before... it was just a massive undertaking for a teaching assistant. 

And honestly, ever since I took over that STEM-Arts initiative eight months ago, this feeling has just been building and building. I kept telling myself, 'Oh, it'll get easier once the first quarter's lesson plans are finalized,' or 'I'll feel better after we get through the parent-teacher conferences,' but I never did. I never got that relief. The stress and this... this heavy, exhausting feeling just kept piling up, day after day. Even on the days where maybe the kids do a really great job building their little engineering projects, and I should be happy or proud of them, I just stand in the back of the classroom feeling completely hollowed out. I just look at the clock and calculate how many hours until I can go back to bed. So, no, I haven't had any periods where I felt better. It’s really just been a straight line down since I took on that curriculum.

patient.answer:
Moderate, I'd say. Or... well, maybe it's hard to put a label on it, but moderate sounds about right. It's not like I'm screaming or crying hysterically all day, but it's just... it's always there. 

Most days, I feel like there's this heavy, gray film over everything. It's like looking at the world through a dirty window, you know? Like, the sun might be shining outside, and the kids might be running around on the playground, laughing and playing, and I can see that they're happy, but I can't feel any of it. I can just be standing right there in the middle of a classroom full of students, or even just sitting at the kitchen table at home with my husband while he's telling me about his day at work, and I still just feel completely hollow inside. 

It's this deep, aching emptiness that just sits right in the middle of my chest. And it's so close to the surface, too. Like, I'll be helping a student mix paint for an art project, or I'll be sorting through the recycling bin to find materials for the STEM modules, and suddenly I just feel so incredibly close to tears. For absolutely no reason! Nothing bad even happened, but the tears are just right there, prickling behind my eyes, and it takes so much energy just to blink them back and keep a straight face for the kids. It’s exhausting, really, carrying that around all the time. It just drains the color out of everything. So, yes, moderate, I suppose, because I can still function, but it's a very heavy, constant sort of sadness.
